text: In 1847 a young lawyer stepped off into Chicago carrying a satchel, a fresh law license, and a dollar and a quarter to his name.
He was born in White Creek, New York, in 1822, a cousin of the Ezra Cornell who would later put his name on a university.
The Chicago he walked into was a muddy boomtown of a few thousand people, hemmed in along the river, planked sidewalks over the mud, the lake at its edge and prairie at its back.
Cornell took work at a law firm his very first day and slept in the office because he had nowhere else to go.
He had no money and no land.
He spent the next six years getting both, and the way he got the land tells you what kind of man he was.
